title: On‑Prem Provisioning Seed Catalog and Certificate Rotation Playbook (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This is a working draft of a short, actionable playbook for two common on‑prem customer scenarios we keep tripping over during handoffs: (1) bootstrapping an air‑gapped or tightly firewalled customer site with a minimal "seed catalog" (images, charts, tf modules) and (2) a safe certificate/key rotation pattern that plays nicely with our private control plane, customer KMS/HSM, and short outage windows.

Scope and audience:
- Audience: solutions engineers, platform SREs, customer engineering.
- Scope: customer onboarding for private deployments (VPC + on‑prem appliance or VM fleet). Not a full runbook for data plane failures; focused on provisioning, seeding, and cert lifecycle.

Quick summary of recommended approach:
1) Create a minimal immutable seed bundle for the customer (images, helm charts, terraform modules, manifests, and a small CA cert bundle if required). Distribute as a tarball and an accompanying signed manifest.
2) Use a two‑phase cert rotation: "prepare" (upload rotated certs to staging store + CI smoke) followed by "cutover" (atomic swap of symlink/secret). Rollback: fast switch to previous symlink/secret.
3) Automate seeding via a small onprem installer component (shell + tiny Go agent) that performs minimal verification and unpacks into the cluster/VMs; avoid heavy orchestration during initial seed.

Prereqs (customer side / ours):
- Customer infra: bootstrap VM/host with outbound HTTPS to our control plane OR offline transfer route (sneakernet / proxy).
- Customer provides: admin contact, CIDR blocks, egress rules, KMS/HSM access details (if used), and an approved list of IPs for allowlist.
- We require: signed seed bundle, terraform modules, a short run of the onboarding smoke tests, and optionally a transient support VPN for initial handoff.

Seed bundle contents (minimal):
- /images/: OCI tar gz of runtime images we need (in order, tagged with semantic tags)
- /charts/: helm charts used for initial deploy (values.yaml examples)
- /tf/: trimmed terraform modules used to provision control-plane resources (only the ones used for networking and bootstrap)
- /manifests/: kube manifests used to install the tiny installer/agent
- /meta/manifest.json (SHA256 checksums + GPG signature)
- README-installation.txt (short, imperative steps)

Create seed bundle (ops notes):
- Build images with CI job: ci/seeds/build-images -> produces images/ and manifests.
- Create manifest.json with structure: { "files": [{"path":"images/runner.tar.gz","sha256":"...","size":...}], "bundle_version":"2025-11-03-seed-v1" } (we store an external copy in s3/backups).
- Sign: gpg --detach-sign --armor manifest.json -> manifest.json.asc
- Tarball: tar czf redwood-seed-<customer>-<date>.tgz images charts tf manifests meta
- Check: sha256sum redwood-seed-*.tgz > bundle.sha256

Installer/agent behavior (tiny, intentionally simple):
- Verify manifest GPG signature locally.
- Unpack bundle into /opt/redwood/seed/ (atomic move).
- Validate checksums of each file.
- If images present, load images via: ctr images import or crictl load (detect runtime).
- For helm charts, run: helm template ./charts/controller -f ./charts/values-onprem.yaml | kubectl apply -f - (but if airgapped use local helm binary).
- Apply minimal network policies if supplied.

Terraform module notes (trimmed, explicit variable surface):
- Modules we check into seed bundle: network/ (vpc + subnets), bastion/, kube-bootstrap/, ingress-proxy/
- Keep modules minimal: no remote state config baked in. Provide examples that use local state with explicit backend stanzas commented out.
- Key variables (recommended): customer_name, region_hint, control_plane_cidrs (list), allowed_admin_ips (list), bootstrap_node_count (int)
- Example module call (in tf root):
  module \"network\" {
    source = \"./tf/modules/network\"
    customer_name = var.customer_name
    control_plane_cidrs = var.control_plane_cidrs
    allowed_admin_ips = var.allowed_admin_ips
  }

Notes on remote/backed state:
- For airgapped installs we prefer: local state + a recommended post-install step to migrate state to a customer S3/GCS or Vault backend (documented sample commands).
- Document an explicit state export/import checklist for customers that insist on a shared remote state (common source of confusion/lockouts).

Certificate rotation pattern (detailed):
Goal: rotate TLS certs (control plane and service-to-service mTLS) with minimal downtime and a single maintenance window under 10 minutes for control plane endpoints.
Principles:
- Always stage new certs and do smoke tests before changing traffic routing.
- Use a pointer/alias to the active key (symlink or secret name like redwood/tls/current) so swaps are atomic.
- Keep at least one previous version available for fast rollback.

Actors & stores supported:
- Customer-managed KMS/HSM (preferred for private installs)
- Vault (HashiCorp) with Transit/PKI
- ACME/ACM (for cloud-connected installs)
- Self-signed / customer CA (allowed if policy requires)

Rotation steps (prepare, test, cutover):
1) Prepare:
  - Generate new keypair in chosen store (example with Vault PKI: vault write pki/issue/redwood common_name=\"control.redwood.customer.local\" ttl=\"8760h\")
  - Export certs in PEM bundle to staging secret store (e.g., k8s secret redwood/tls/staging-v2) and label with metadata: created_at, who, source_kms.
  - Run CI smoke tests against a staging endpoint: curl --cacert staging-ca.pem https://control-plane-staging:8443/health -> expect 200 and X-Redwood-Version header.
2) Cutover (scheduled maintenance):
  - Ensure cluster control-plane nodes in maintenance mode (drain optional non-control nodes)
  - Atomically rename secrets/symlink: kubectl annotate secret redwood-tls current=staging-v2; change service/ingress to reference secret redwood-tls/current name.
  - Wait 30s, run smoke tests. If failure -> rollback path.
3) Post-cutover validation:
  - Run end‑to‑end smoke (auth, DB write, sample generation).
  - Confirm metrics and alerting; maintain rollback window of 60 minutes.

Rollback (fast):
- If smoke tests fail, switch the pointer back to previous secret: annotate back or update the symlink. Because clients often cache certs, keep previous cert's validity overlap at least 72 hours.

Edge cases and gotchas:
- Customers that rely on short cert TTLs (1–4 hours) may trigger cascade issues; recommend minimum overlap >= 72h during rotation windows.
- HSM: export rules often prevent private key extraction. In that case we rely on the store performing signing; the cutover must update the pointer to the public cert. Test early with a lab HSM.
- Older clients may not follow SNI correctly; keep legacy ingress in path during migration.

Upgrade plan for control plane (phased) — recommended timeline for customers with strict change control:
Phase A (prework, 1–2 weeks): collect baselines (metrics, traffic patterns), prepare seed bundle, validate remote access.
Phase B (staging exercise, 1 day): deploy seed bundle into staging mimic of customer infra (or our internal lab), complete smoke tests, record roll-forward and rollback steps.
Phase C (maintenance window, 2–4 hours): perform cert cutover and minor runtime upgrade, follow immediate validation checks.
Phase D (post upgrade monitoring, 48–72 hours): watch SLOs and errors, scheduled follow up call with customer.

Troubleshooting cheat sheet (fast path):
- Installer fails on gpg verification: re-download manifest.asc, check gpg --verify, ensure correct key fingerprint (key: 0xA1B2C3D4).
- Images fail to load: check runtime (containerd vs crio vs docker). Use crictl images, ctr images import, or docker load accordingly.
- TF apply stuck waiting for provider auth: run TF_LOG=TRACE and check provider configuration; common miss: missing customer API key or VPC peering permission.

Operational play examples (commands):
- Verify bundle signature:
  gpg --keyring ./trustedkeys.gpg --verify manifest.json.asc manifest.json
- Load image (containerd):
  sudo ctr -n k8s.io images import images/runtime.tar.gz
- Create staging secret from cert bundle:
  kubectl create secret tls redwood-tls-staging-v2 --cert=cert.pem --key=key.pem -n redwood || kubectl replace secret ...

Notes to self / open questions:
- Should we include a tiny built-in web UI to show bundle content and checksums? (pros: reduces operator errors; cons: increases attack surface for airgapped installs).
- Decide canonical way to represent pointer to active cert: symlink file path vs k8s secret name vs configmap entry. Right now k8s secret name annotation is easiest.
- Need a sample policy for HSM providers listing allowed export operations. Add to seed bundle FAQ.
- Talk to legal about required language for customer-supplied CAs / liability if we provide sample self‑signed CA files.

Appendix A — Example minimal terraform snippet (customer root):
# variables.tf
# variable \"customer_name\" { default = \"acme-corp\" }
# main.tf
provider \"local\" {}
module \"bootstrap_network\" {
  source = \"./tf/modules/network\"
  customer_name = var.customer_name
  control_plane_cidrs = [\"10.0.0.0/24\"]
  allowed_admin_ips = [\"203.0.113.5/32\"]
}

Appendix B — Rapid checklist for supports calls (10‑minute read):
- Confirm bundle version and signature.
- Confirm images loaded & pods are in CrashLoopBackoff? get logs.
- Verify cert pointers and run curl healthcheck with -k or --cacert.
- If rollback required: restore secret pointer and notify customer to restart clients if needed.

References / links (internal):
- Confluence: ONPREM Seed Catalog (linked above)
- Internal lab repo: github.com/redwood-inference/private-deployments/seed-lab
- Incident: ENGPD-1301 (failed cert rotation postmortem)

TODOs (short):

- [ ] Draft customer-facing handoff checklist for SOC/Network teams

End of draft.
